title: How do you read a waterfall chart in a case interview?
description: How waterfall charts show what moved a number from one value to another, how to read them quickly, the common traps, and a worked profit bridge.
hook: Read a waterfall chart by noting the start value, end value and total change, then finding the one or two bars that explain most of that change, and saying what to investigate next. Waterfalls, also called bridge charts, are a consultant favourite because they answer the question every profit case asks: what changed?
body:
What a waterfall shows

A starting value sits on the left and an ending value on the right. In between, floating bars show each increase or decrease, so you can see how you got from one to the other. Increases step up, decreases step down, and together they bridge the gap exactly.

Typical case uses: profit last year versus this year, budget versus actual, or revenue broken down into price, volume and mix effects.

How to read one in 30 seconds

  1. Read the frame. Start and end values, units and the time period. Is this $M or $k? One year or five?
  2. State the total change. "Profit fell by $3M, or 30%."
  3. Find the biggest bar, up or down.
  4. Group the bars. Revenue drivers versus cost drivers, or controllable versus external. Several small bars in one group can matter more than one big bar elsewhere.
  5. Check the bars reconcile. If they do not add up to the end value, a bar, a sign or an adjustment is missing.
  6. Say what explains most of the change, and what to look at next.

A worked example

A food manufacturer's profit fell from $10M to $7M. The bars in between are:

DriverEffect on profit
Price+$1.0M
Volume−$0.5M
Ingredients−$1.5M
Wages−$1.0M
Energy−$1.0M

Check: $10M + $1M − $0.5M − $1.5M − $1M − $1M = $7M. It reconciles.

Group them. The revenue side (price and volume) is net +$0.5M. The cost side (ingredients, wages and energy) is −$3.5M. So costs explain more than the whole fall, and ingredients are the largest single driver.

Strong: "Profit fell $3M, and costs explain all of it: $3.5M of extra cost, led by $1.5M on ingredients, more than offset a $1M gain from price. I'd start with ingredients: is it commodity prices, a supplier change or more waste?"
Weak: "Price went up by one, volume went down by half a million, ingredients went down by 1.5, wages by one, energy by one."

The weak answer reads every bar in order and leaves the interviewer to do the thinking. The strong one gives the total, groups the bars, names the biggest and proposes a next step.

Watch the price and volume bars

When price and volume both change, the split between them depends on the method, and it is easy to double count. Suppose a product's price rises from $10 to $11 while volume falls from 1.0M to 0.95M units. Revenue goes from $10M to $10.45M, a $0.45M gain.

  • Price effect at the old volume: $1 × 1.0M = +$1.0M.
  • Volume effect at the old price: −50,000 × $10 = −$0.5M.
  • Those sum to +$0.5M, so there is a −$0.05M interaction term ($1 × −50,000) to make it reconcile.

Some bridges fold the interaction into one of the bars instead, for example by valuing the price effect at the new volume (0.95M × $1 = $0.95M) and the volume effect at the old price (−$0.5M), which gives exactly $0.45M. Either is fine. What is not fine is valuing both effects at the new figures, which gives $0.95M − $0.55M = $0.40M and quietly loses $50k. If the bars in a case do not reconcile, ask which baseline was used.

Common traps

  • Describing every bar in order instead of leading with the total and the biggest driver.
  • Missing that small bars add up. Three modest supply-chain bars can outweigh one large labour bar.
  • Ignoring the units and period. A $2M bar over five years is a very different story from $2M in one year.
  • Treating every bar as actionable. A cost rise from commodity prices calls for a different response from one caused by waste. Say which bars the client can control.

Practice

1. Revenue went from $50M to $56M. The bridge shows price +$4M, volume +$5M, mix −$1M and one bar labelled "currency" with no number. What is it?

Show the answer

$56M − $50M − $4M − $5M + $1M = −$2M. Currency movements cost the client $2M, which means the underlying business grew faster than the headline 12% suggests.

2. Costs rose from $30M to $36M: raw materials +$1.5M, freight +$1.2M, packaging +$1.3M, labour +$2.0M. Where would you look first?

Show the answer

Labour is the biggest single bar, but raw materials, freight and packaging are all supply-chain costs and add up to $4.0M, two-thirds of the $6M rise. A strong answer groups them: "Two-thirds of the increase is supply chain, so I'd start with procurement and logistics, then come back to labour."

Where to practise next
